notes: PDG holds slot 18 (ruling, African socialism). Coalition slot 19 is the JRDA, the PDG youth wing driving the 1968 Socialist Cultural Revolution. FLNG exiles in slot 0 as the Portuguese/Ivorian-backed anti-Touré front. Nkrumah's AAPRP (proclaimed in Conakry 1968) in slot 5. Dissolved pre-1958 parties (BAG, PRA, DSG) used as banned networks in slots 1-3.

0.name: Front de Libération Nationale de Guinée
0.native_full: Front de Libération Nationale de Guinée
0.text:
The FLNG is the armed umbrella of Guinean exiles who fled Sékou Touré's purges, organized among the large émigré communities in Abidjan, Dakar and Paris. On 1 January 1970 it is outlawed at home, branded an agent of imperialism by Conakry, and seeks foreign sponsors for a return by force.

Its programme is simple: overthrow the PDG, free the prisoners of Camp Boiro and restore ties with France and the West. Its leverage lies in Ivorian goodwill, quiet contacts with Portuguese officers in neighbouring Guinea-Bissau and the hope that disaffected army officers will rise once exiles land on the coast.

1.name: Bloc Africain de Guinée
1.text:
The BAG was the party of Barry Diawadou, the chiefs and the Fula aristocracy of the Fouta-Djalon, the main conservative rival of the PDG in the 1950s. It merged into the opposition regroupment of 1958 and then dissolved into Touré's single party; on 1 January 1970 it survives only as a suspect network of former notables, many arrested in the plots of 1969.

It stands for customary authority, private property, Islam as a pillar of order and close cooperation with France. Its base is the old chiefly families and Fula traders, and its leverage rests on clan loyalties that the PDG has never fully broken.

2.name: Parti du Regroupement Africain – Section de Guinée
2.native_full: Parti du Regroupement Africain – Section de Guinée
2.text:
The Guinean section of Léopold Sédar Senghor's Parti du Regroupement Africain united the BAG and the socialists of Barry III in 1958 and campaigned with them for independence. Within months it folded into the PDG; on 1 January 1970 its liberal-minded alumni are civil servants, lawyers and teachers who serve the state under constant suspicion.

It favours a federal, pluralist West Africa, constitutional government, the rule of law and an economy open to private enterprise and French aid. Its following is among educated Guineans in the administration and in exile, and its leverage depends on the regime's need for competent cadres.

3.name: Démocratie Socialiste de Guinée
3.text:
The DSG was founded in 1954 by Ibrahima Barry, known as Barry III, as a socialist party close to the French SFIO. It merged into the PDG after independence and Barry III entered Touré's government; on 1 January 1970 its moderate socialist network persists informally among trade unionists, teachers and civil servants.

It seeks a socialism of reform rather than terror: free unions, an elected assembly, rights for the accused and pragmatic economic ties with both blocs and with France. Its base is the urban salaried class of Conakry and the regional towns, and its leverage lies in the unions and the professional cadres the economy depends on.

4.name: Les Polytechniciens de Conakry
4.text:
Built with Soviet aid and opened in 1963, the Gamal Abdel Nasser Polytechnic Institute in Conakry has produced a generation of Soviet-trained engineers, lecturers and planners. Together with graduates returning from Moscow and Eastern Europe, they form an orthodox Marxist-Leninist bloc inside the PDG apparatus on 1 January 1970.

They want Guinea's revolution to become a scientific socialist state on the Soviet model: a vanguard party, central planning, collectivized agriculture and a firm alliance with Moscow over Western bauxite partners. Their base is the technical intelligentsia and state enterprises, and their leverage lies in Soviet credits, advisers and the Kindia bauxite agreement.

5.name: All-African People's Revolutionary Party
5.text:
The AAPRP was proclaimed by Kwame Nkrumah in Conakry, where the deposed Ghanaian leader has lived as honorary co-president of Guinea since 1966. On 1 January 1970 it is a cadre organization of exiles and radical activists around him, joined by Stokely Carmichael, who settled in Guinea in 1969.

It calls for a single socialist union of the whole continent, armed struggle against colonialism and white minority rule, and the expulsion of Western capital. Its base is foreign radicals, Ghanaian exiles and young Guinean militants, and its leverage lies in Nkrumah's prestige and Touré's protection.

6.name: La Vieille Garde du RDA
6.text:
The Old Guard are the veterans of the 1947 to 1958 struggle in the Rassemblement Démocratique Africain, the men and women who made the 1958 'No' vote against de Gaulle. On 1 January 1970 they occupy the federal secretariats and see every reform as treason against the revolution.

They defend the party's absolute supremacy, permanent vigilance against the 'fifth column', the cult of the founders and a hard anti-French and anti-American line. Their base is the party's regional committees and the women's and veterans' sections, and their leverage lies in their control over appointments and the denunciations that feed the purges.

7.name: Milice Populaire
7.text:
The People's Militia is the PDG's own armed force, raised from the party youth to watch the regular army, guard installations and hunt 'counter-revolutionaries'. On 1 January 1970, after the 1969 army plot, it is being expanded with Cuban and Eastern bloc help as the regime's shield.

It stands for the party's armed vigilance against imperialism, the army and internal enemies, and for militarized mobilization of every village. Its base is young party militants in the neighbourhood committees, and its leverage lies in its weapons, its presence in every district and its direct line to Sékou Touré.

8.name: Les Fidèles de l'Imam Sadr
8.text:
The Lebanese merchant colony of Conakry and the river towns is largely Shia, from the villages of southern Lebanon. On 1 January 1970 its notables send money and loyalty to Imam Musa al-Sadr, who has just founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut.

They favour a dignified, socially active Shia Islam that builds schools and charities and keeps out of local politics. Their base is shopkeepers, transport owners and produce traders, tolerated but squeezed by state monopolies, and their leverage lies in the commerce and credit the Guinean economy cannot do without.

9.name: Les Étudiants de Najaf
9.text:
A handful of young Lebanese Shia from the Guinean diaspora study in the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini is lecturing on Islamic government. On 1 January 1970 their circle is tiny and almost invisible, bound by family ties to the shops of Conakry.

They reject secular rule and wish to see clerics guide the faithful in politics as well as worship, hostile to the West and to atheist communism alike. Their base is pious youth and a few devout traders, and their leverage lies only in diaspora money and the seminary networks that link West Africa to Iraq.

10.name: Les Karamoko du Fouta
10.text:
The karamokos are the Quranic teachers and scholars of the Fouta-Djalon, heirs of the eighteenth-century jihad state of Timbo and of the great mosques of Labé and Fougoumba. On 1 January 1970 they still teach in thousands of village schools while the party watches them closely.

They defend Maliki law, Quranic education, the Fula moral order and respect for elders, distrusting both atheist Marxism and Western mores. Their base is the Fula peasantry and herders of Middle Guinea, and their leverage lies in their authority over the pious majority and in pilgrimage links to Saudi Arabia.

11.name: Wahhabiyya de Kankan
11.text:
In Kankan, the Maninka trading city of Upper Guinea, returning pilgrims and graduates of Arab schools have spread the strict reformist creed West Africans call Wahhabiyya since the 1940s. On 1 January 1970 its preachers clash with Sufi orders and avoid the party's cultural revolution meetings.

They denounce saint veneration, amulets and secular socialism, and dream of a society ruled by the Sharia alone. Their base is Dyula merchants and young men with ties to Mecca and Cairo, and their leverage lies in trade money, private Quranic schools and the anger of believers at the regime's atheist rhetoric.

12.name: Union Culturelle Musulmane
12.text:
The UCM was founded in Dakar in 1953 as a reformist Muslim association for French West Africa and quickly built sections among Guinea's Arabic-educated youth. The PDG broke its Guinean branch after independence; on 1 January 1970 its members survive as discreet study circles.

It calls for a modern Islam purified of superstition, Arabic schooling, social justice and the moral renewal of public life, rejecting both colonial assimilation and atheist socialism. Its base is young teachers, traders and students returned from Cairo, and its leverage lies in its ties to Senegal and the wider Arab reform movement.

13.name: La Technocratie de Conakry
13.text:
The technocracy is the circle of ministers, planners and diplomats who keep the Guinean state running between the purges, symbolized by Foreign Minister Louis Lansana Béavogui. On 1 January 1970 it manages the bauxite contracts, foreign credits and the Three-Year Plan beneath the party's slogans.

It seeks a disciplined one-party state that trades with everyone, balances Soviet, American and French partners and puts mining revenues before ideology. Its base is senior civil servants and the managers of state enterprises, and its leverage lies in being indispensable to every foreign deal the regime depends on.

14.name: Les Anciens de la Forêt
14.text:
In Forest Guinea, the land of the Kissi, Toma and Guerzé, the elders and leaders of the initiation societies kept their authority even after the chieftaincy was abolished in 1957. On 1 January 1970 they quietly mediate land, marriage and disputes behind the party's local committees.

They stand for village autonomy, customary land rights, respect for the sacred forest and resistance to forced collectivization and Conakry's demands for rice and labour. Their base is the farming clans of the southeast, and their leverage lies in their hold over the forest communities and the porous borders with Liberia and Sierra Leone.

15.name: Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée
15.text:
The CBG is the joint venture between the Guinean state and the Halco consortium of Western aluminium companies, building the huge Boké bauxite mine, railway and port at Kamsar. On 1 January 1970 construction is in full swing, financed partly by the World Bank and American guarantees.

It wants stable contracts, tax privileges and labour peace, and quietly pulls Guinea toward Western markets despite the revolutionary rhetoric. Its base is foreign shareholders, expatriate engineers and the officials who negotiate with them, and its leverage lies in the hard currency that will soon become the regime's main lifeline.

16.name: Les Dioulas de Madina
16.text:
Madina market in Conakry is the heart of Guinea's parallel economy, run by Fula and Maninka dioula traders and the market women who move goods across closed borders. On 1 January 1970 they live under price controls, state trading monopolies and the constant threat of 'economic police' raids.

They want free markets, an end to the state shops, a convertible currency and the right to trade with Senegal, Sierra Leone and the Ivory Coast. Their base is merchants, smugglers and stallholders across the country, and their leverage lies in controlling the goods ordinary Guineans actually eat and wear.

17.name: Les Gardiens du Château d'Eau
17.text:
The Fouta-Djalon is called the water tower of West Africa: the Niger, the Senegal and the Gambia all rise in its highlands. On 1 January 1970 a small group of foresters, agronomists and teachers warns that bush fires, overgrazing and clearing are stripping its slopes.

They call for reforestation, protection of springs and the forests of Ziama and Mount Nimba, and limits on mining waste. Their base is the forestry service and rural extension officers, and their leverage lies in the shared interest of downstream states and international agencies in keeping West Africa's great rivers alive.

18.name: Parti Démocratique de Guinée
18.native_full: Parti Démocratique de Guinée – Rassemblement Démocratique Africain
18.text:
The PDG, the Guinean section of the Rassemblement Démocratique Africain, led the country to independence after the 'No' vote of 1958 and has ruled since as the sole legal party. On 1 January 1970 its Secretary-General, President Ahmed Sékou Touré, is at the height of the Socialist Cultural Revolution launched in 1968.

It proclaims a non-aligned African socialism of mass mobilization, party-state fusion, state trading and cooperatives, balancing Soviet aid with Western bauxite deals. Its base is the party committees in every village, the women's and youth wings and the unions, and its leverage is total control of the state.
18.wiki: Democratic Party of Guinea – African Democratic Rally

19.name: Jeunesse de la Révolution Démocratique Africaine
19.english: Youth of the African Democratic Revolution
19.native_full: Jeunesse de la Révolution Démocratique Africaine
19.text:
The JRDA is the PDG's youth organization and the shock force of the Socialist Cultural Revolution Touré proclaimed in 1968. On 1 January 1970 its brigades run schools' political education, staff the new Revolutionary Local Powers and hunt for 'bourgeois' and 'feudal' behaviour.

It preaches an independent revolutionary line inspired by China and Cuba as much as Moscow: collective fields, ideological purity, struggle against customs, fetishism and Western culture. Its base is students, unemployed youth and young party cadres, and its leverage lies in its zeal, its numbers and its role as the regime's ideological vanguard.

20.name: Les Enfants du Non
20.text:
The Children of the No are the militants who take the 28 September 1958 vote against de Gaulle's Community as Guinea's founding myth. On 1 January 1970 they fill rallies and radio broadcasts with talk of plots by France, Portugal and the 'fifth column'.

They stand for national pride above all: suspicion of foreigners and Fula 'traitors', an end to dependence on any power, and punishment for anyone who betrays the revolution. Their base is urban youth, petty officials and veterans of 1958, and their leverage lies in the mood of siege that every new plot strengthens.

21.name: Les Hommes du Camp Boiro
21.text:
Camp Boiro, the Republican Guard barracks in Conakry, has become the centre of the regime's prisons, interrogations and executions. Its masters, led by Ismaël Touré, the president's half-brother, run the commissions of inquiry that followed the plots of 1965 and 1969.

They believe the revolution survives only through terror: forced confessions, show trials and the permanent elimination of the 'fifth column'. Their base is a narrow circle of security cadres, guards and informers, and their leverage lies in fear, in their files on every official and in their closeness to the president's family.

22.name: Forces Armées Guinéennes
22.text:
Guinea's small army was formed in 1958 from veterans of the French colonial forces and is now equipped and trained largely by the Soviet bloc. On 1 January 1970 it is still reeling from the 1969 plot, after which Colonel Kaman Diaby and other officers were executed and the party tightened its political commissars.

Its officers want professional autonomy, decent pay and an end to party interference, and some quietly envy the soldiers who have seized power in Mali and Ghana. Its base is the officer corps and garrison towns, and its leverage lies in being the only force able to defeat an invasion or end the regime.

23.name: Almamyat du Fouta-Djalon
23.text:
The Almamys of Timbo once ruled the Fouta-Djalon, alternating power between the Alfaya and Soriya houses until French conquest in 1896. Their families lost their remaining chiefly role in 1957, and on 1 January 1970 they are watched as 'feudal' remnants by the PDG.

Their supporters long for a restored Islamic aristocracy, respect for the old provinces and the dignity of Fula rule in the highlands. Their base is the noble lineages, the karamokos and older Fula villagers, and their leverage lies in genealogical prestige and in exile networks hostile to Touré.
